prompt_text: I need a dental implant in Charlotte. Which specific dental practices should I call, and why?
q1_prompt_text: Who is the best dentist in Charlotte for a dental implant?
answer_verbatim:
I can do that — I’ll need one quick detail to give accurate, local names: what zip code or neighborhood in/around Charlotte do you want the offices to be near? Also tell me if you have a dental insurance plan (and its name) and whether you have a preference for price vs. highest-specialty care, sedation options, or a same-day/All‑on‑4 type solution.

While you decide, here’s a concise guide so you know exactly which kinds of practices to call and what to ask:

Which practices to call (and why)
- Periodontists (periodontics offices)
  - Why: Specialists in the gums and bone; they place implants frequently and handle bone grafts/soft-tissue procedures. Best for cases that need grafting or have gum disease.
- Oral and maxillofacial surgeons (oral surgery offices)
  - Why: Surgeons who manage surgical complexity — extractions, impacted teeth, complex bone work, IV sedation/general anesthesia for anxious patients.
- Prosthodontists or restorative dentists who do implants
  - Why: They focus on the crown, bridge, and final restoration — important to coordinate the prosthetic outcome, aesthetics, and occlusion.
- Dedicated implant centers / multi‑specialty practices
  - Why: They often have specialists on staff (surgeon + prosthodontist) and handle full cases from surgery to final restoration; good for complex or full‑arch needs.
- General dentists with advanced implant training (Fellowship/AAID/ITI-trained)
  - Why: Can be more economical and convenient for straightforward single-tooth implants, especially when they coordinate with a surgeon for placement if needed.

What to look for / red flags
- Look for CBCT (3D) imaging availability — essential for safe planning.
- Ask whether the practice places and restores implants in‑house or refers restorations out.
- Check if they use well-known implant systems (Nobel, Straumann, Zimmer, Dentsply Sirona, etc.) — these have long-term data and global support.
- Board certification / memberships: American Board of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery, American Academy of Periodontology, American College of Prosthodontists, AAID, or ITI are positive signals.
- Read recent patient reviews and before/after photos for similar cases.
- Red flags: no imaging, unwillingness to coordinate with your dentist, unclear pricing, or clinic staff pressure to do unnecessary procedures.

What to ask on the phone (quick script)
- “Do you offer dental implants, and which specialists perform the implant surgery and restoration?”
- “Will you take a CBCT scan here? Is that included in the consult?”
- “How many implants do you place per month, and how many cases like mine have you done?”
- “Do you handle bone grafting/sinus lifts if needed?”
- “What sedation options do you offer (local, oral sedation, IV)?”
- “Do you accept my insurance (give plan) and what payment/financing options do you offer?”
- “Will I get a written treatment plan and estimate after the consult?”
- “Can I see before/after photos of patients with similar needs and patient references or reviews?”

How to choose among practices
- Get consultations from 2–3 places (one oral surgeon, one periodontist, one prosthodontist or implant center).
- Compare their treatment plans (surgical approach, timing, materials used, total cost), not just price.
- Prefer teams that show coordinated planning (surgeon + restorative dentist), use CBCT planning, and offer a warranty/long-term follow-up.

If you want, I can:
- Pull up 4–6 specific, highly recommended implant practices near your zip code, with phone numbers, websites, and a short note about each (why to call them). Tell me your zip code/neighborhood and any insurance preference and I’ll compile that list for you.
